title: Molarity, Molality, Normality: Solution Concentration Units
h1: Solution concentration — molarity, molality and normality
description: Molarity (mol/L) uses solution volume. Molality (mol/kg) uses solvent mass. Normality is molarity × valence. Miss the difference and titrations fail.

author.name: The Turbo Unit Converter engineering desk

reviewer.name: Turbo Unit Converter editorial review

hero: M and m look alike, act differently. Molality is invariant with temperature; molarity is not. Freezing-point depression uses molality. Volumetric titration uses molarity.
body: Concentration has three common measurements because each is invariant with respect to different variables. Temperature swells solutions, adding water changes total volume — the choice of denominator determines which experiment your number survives.

> Molarity M = moles solute / L solution
> Molality m = moles solute / kg solvent
> Normality N = M × equivalents per mole (varies by reaction context)
> For dilute aqueous solutions near 25 °C: M ≈ m

Molarity: volumetric titration, most bench chemistry, pharmaceutical dilutions. Molality: colligative properties (freezing point, osmotic pressure), high-precision physical chemistry. Normality: acid-base titrations of polyprotic acids, redox chemistry.

1 mol NaCl in 1 kg water = 1 m. ΔT_f = i × K_f × m = 2 × 1.86 × 1 = 3.72 °C depression. Use 1 M (in 1 L solution, less than 1 kg water) and you get a slightly different ΔT because the water mass is off — small at 1 M, large at 5 M.
M is per litre solution. m is per kg solvent. N is context-dependent.

faqs.a: Above ~0.1 M for aqueous, or any concentrated non-aqueous solution. Also at extreme temperatures where density shifts.

faqs.q: Is 1 N HCl the same as 1 M HCl?
faqs.a: Yes — HCl is monoprotic. But 1 N H₂SO₄ is 0.5 M (2 acidic protons per mole).
